one_liner: Branch-free 64-bit unsigned divide and modulo via a Newton-Raphson reciprocal; claims about 30% faster than hardware div on Intel.
what_it_does: A single header, fast-divide.h, with FastDivide(N, D), FastModulo(N, D) and FastDivMod(N, D, rem) for arbitrary runtime uint64_t operands, plus a FastDivider class that precomputes a reciprocal once and then offers Divide, Modulo and DivMod for many numerators. These are function calls, not operator replacements; they cover only unsigned 64-bit values and leave division by zero undefined (no trap). GCC and Clang (including clang-cl) get hand-written AT&T inline assembly; MSVC gets an intrinsic-based C version (__umulh, _addcarry_u64, _lzcnt_u64).
how_it_is_fast: It replaces the microcoded DIV with multiplies: lzcnt plus two BMI2 shifts (shlx/shrx) give a 2-bit-accurate first guess of floor(2^64/D) from a first-order expansion around the normalized divisor, five Newton-Raphson steps (M += umulh(M, -M*D)) double the correct bits up to 64, and a multiply-high by N gives a quotient at most 2 below the true one, corrected with add/cmov/adc instead of branches. There are no table lookups or branches, so the cost does not depend on the operands; FastDivider hoists the Newton steps out of the loop, so each later divide is one mul, one imul and a carry fix-up. The standalone path is a serial chain of about a dozen 64-bit multiplies, so it can only win where DIV r64 is slow (42-95 cycles latency on Skylake per Agner Fog's tables, as quoted in a search snippet).
when_to_use: Latency-bound 64-bit unsigned division by divisors that change from call to call, on Intel cores of the Haswell-to-Skylake-derivative generation where DIV r64 is slow (the README hedges: 'at least on Intel').
Code that needs data-independent timing for 64-bit division (the README's crypto use case), built with GCC or Clang so the branch-free inline-asm path is used.
A divisor reused a handful of times, where FastDivider's setup (one Newton sequence, no branching on divisor class) is cheaper than heavier precomputation schemes.
Hot loops with spare registers: the asm pins N to rcx, D to rdx and the result to rax and needs two more scratch registers.
when_not_to_use: Recent CPUs with fast dividers: search snippets give DIV r64 latency of about 14-18 cycles on Rocket Lake and Alder Lake-P (uops.info) and 9-17 cycles on Zen 3, well under this routine's chain of about a dozen serial multiplies, so it is probably slower there; benchmark before adopting.
Divisors known at compile time (the README itself says the compiler's multiply-shift codegen is better) or a divisor reused millions of times (libdivide or fastmod).
Register-starved inner loops: the README warns that spills caused by the extra registers can erase the gain.
Signed or 32-bit division, non-x86-64 targets, or x86 CPUs without LZCNT and BMI2 (pre-Haswell Intel, pre-Excavator AMD); no runtime CPU check exists.
Code that relies on a divide-by-zero trap: the result is simply undefined.

integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (<cstdint>); GCC or Clang with LZCNT enabled for the _lzcnt_u64 intrinsic in FastDivider (e.g. -mlzcnt or -march=haswell or later; the author's own test in issue #1 used -march=skylake); MSVC x64 for the C fallback. No build files, tests or benchmark in the repo.
integration.platforms: x86-64 only; CPU must support LZCNT and BMI2 (Intel Haswell or later, AMD Excavator/Zen or later); any x86-64 OS with GCC, Clang or MSVC
integration.thread_safety: Not documented; the functions are pure and FastDivider is immutable after construction, so concurrent const use is safe by construction.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: FastDivide/FastModulo/FastDivMod calls replace N / D and N % D for uint64_t only; no operator overloads, no signed or 32-bit versions, and division by zero is undefined instead of trapping

gotchas: FastDivider::GetDivisor() returns the stored member m_D, which the constructor sets to (uint64_t)-(int64_t)divisor, so FastDivider(7).GetDivisor() returns 2^64 - 7, not 7 (API bug in the current header; Divide/Modulo/DivMod are unaffected).

No CPU feature check: on CPUs without LZCNT the lzcnt encoding executes as bsr and silently yields a different count, after which the GCC/Clang asm path faults on shlx (no BMI2) and the MSVC path, which uses ordinary shifts unless built for AVX2, would return untrustworthy quotients instead of crashing.

The MSVC fallback computes E >>= C with C = 2^64 - lzcnt(D), a shift count of 64 or more that is undefined behavior in C++ and only works because x86 masks shift counts; the author's own comments call its codegen 'super dumb' (branches), so neither the speed nor the constant-time claim is assured on MSVC.

FastDivider::Modulo returned wrong results until the 2021-02-17 fix (cmovc %[D] changed to cmovc %[N]); the standalone functions were unaffected. Issue #1's wrong results came from the reporter's own C refactor (1 << t instead of 1ULL << t), not the library.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over libdivide or fastmod when the divisor changes on nearly every call and you want a branch-free, constant-time 64-bit divide on an older Intel core; when one divisor is reused many times, libdivide (precomputed magic numbers, up to 10x claimed for 64-bit, SIMD variants) or fastmod (32-bit operands) fit better, and for 128-bit operands use the same author's FastDivide128.
verified_claims_summary: The README asserts 'About 30% faster' than the hardware 64-bit div 'at least on Intel' with no benchmark code, CPU model, compiler version, operand distribution or latency-versus-throughput distinction; the only timings the author posted (issue #1: C path 0.310 vs inline-asm path 0.283, units and CPU unstated) compare the library with itself. Correctness, not speed, was checked here with a Python model of the GCC/Clang asm path: exact quotients and remainders for 660,231 (N, D) pairs over 191,217 divisors, including every divisor within 300 of a power of two, with the class's reciprocal equal to floor(2^64/D) (saturated at 2^64-1 for D = 1) in every case.
status_note: Abandoned since a 2021-09-30 README edit (last code change 2021-02-17); MIT-licensed, a single 13 KB header that is easy to vendor, but benchmark it on your own CPU first, since the 30% claim predates the fast 64-bit dividers in Ice Lake-era Intel and Zen 3 and may well be reversed there.
